correctness.rationale: The full GP(n,2) metric is unambiguously defined. Graph-distance paths lift to a cyclic 2-layer integer cover; path reordering establishes each exact displacement formula. Symmetric anchored Gram matrices of order 2n-1 have exact integer factorizations with nonnegative real roots at n=5,6,9,10, giving squared Euclidean ranks 5,7,9,10. Each other n=7,...,17 has an explicit positive zero-sum distance quadratic vector; the 8-vertex vector on indices 0,2,5,7 gives value 2 for every n>=18 by the nonzero winding bound |delta+mn|>=11. Thus Schoenberg equivalence proves the if-and-only-if statement; exact-integer checker reconstructs graph, determinants and witnesses. No computational finite sample is used as proof of the infinite range.

originality.rationale: The comparison concerns implication of the exact graph-distance CND iff n in {5,6,9,10}, not mere family/name similarity. Full relevant parts of the 2005 distance-balancedness, 2011 general negative-type, adjacency spectrum, 2015 strong metric dimension and 2023 GP(n,2) distance-index papers do not give this classification or imply it via their stated results. A related published published-finding corpus Rips-homotopy claim has no implication for CND. Adjacent metrics from related graph families do not cover GP(n,2). Unseen equivalent historical formulations remain a limited originality risk.
residual_risks: An equivalent characterization may occur under a different name in older distance-matrix, graph embedding, or circulant association-scheme literature.

value.rationale: A canonical infinite family of nontrivial cubic graphs is completely classified by a natural finite-group harmonic-analysis kernel admissibility problem. The four isolated positive cases, minimal squared-Euclidean embedding ranks and a single uniform 8-point signed-distance obstruction for every sufficiently large order are structural, reusable mathematical statements. Their precise data are not routine consequences of the compared adjacency spectra, ordinary graph-metric dimensions or distance-distribution results.
